confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Because of sweeping external sandhi phenomena, the smallest phonetic group of Tunica is the phrase, which may contain a single word or several words. Phrases are always set off from other phrases by pauses and are also characterized by special intonational or melodic features. On the other hand, words occurring within the same phrase form a unit. They are not set off from each other by pauses nor…

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding Haas 1940:13 sentence and the §1.1 domain passage are verbatim in the Rosetta scan we hold scanned; the Haas 1940:28 stress-shift quotations are verbatim in held Bakovic 2016 fn. 10, which is exactly the second-hand route the record declares. Deciding source: Haas's 1940/41 HAIL reference grammar (143 pp.), the top Glottolog descriptive reference and, given that the last speaker died in 1948 and the only recordings are unusable (Tulane TLP page, downloaded), the best description that can ever exist; Bakovic 2016 is a competent phonology article that states it verified every datum against Haas 1940/1953. So the classification rests on the right source and nothing found suggests the stem-initial/never-consecutive generalization is wrong (Wikipedia's Haas paraphrase and the Alcantara 2014 abstract are consistent/silent). Why 'adequate' rather
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: independently re-done. (1) Haas 1940:13 —, Chapter I §1.1 General Remarks, end of 2nd paragraph: 'A phrase or a word may have one or more stressed syllables but these are never con- secutive.' verbatim, and the the domain quotation passage ('Because of sweeping external sandhi phenomena, the smallest phonetic group of Tunica is the phrase..') is the opening of the same §1.1, verbatim. The held Rosetta items are complete as published (archive.org rosettaproject_tun_phon-1 and _detail-1 each imagecount 4; file sizes 180861/5513 and 187441/7029 bytes match the held copies exactly), so nothing more of Haas 1940 is open on archiv

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tunica language' (plain-text extract via MediaWiki API, 2026-09-16); tertiary, its phonology section paraphrases Haas 1940.
sources.quote: 'All stems have an intrinsic stress, and some affixes have intrinsic stress on the first syllable. In the combination of elements to form words and phrases, the stresses are retained if possible, but two stressed syllables do not occur consecutively ... a stem, combined with a stressed monosyllabic prefix, loses its stress.' Tertiary; consistent with the record's prule (stem-initial + inherently stressed affixes + clash repair).

sources.citation: Tunica Language Project (Tulane University / Tunica-Biloxi Tribe). 'Abstracts', Conference on Language Revitalization: Sleeping and Awakened Languages of the Gulf South, March 7-9 2014 — abstract of Alcantara, Craig, 'Stress in Tunica Word Formation and Noun Derivation'.
sources.quote: 'Haas describes stress behavior in detail through a series of examples and rules, and her accompanying Tunica Dictionary, published in 1953, meticulously records the stress pattern of every captured Tunica word. These texts comprise the majority of the corpus and the definitive grammar of the Tunica language.' No rule stated; the paper itself is unpublished.

sources.citation: Tunica Language Project (Tulane). 'About the Tunica Language' web page.
sources.quote: No stress statement. Establishes that Haas's wax-cylinder recordings of Youchigant are unusable ('so inundated with static that the words have become indistinguishable ... leaving no audio sample of a native speaker'), so no instrumental study of Tunica stress can exist and Haas's grammar, texts and dictionary remain the primary resources.
